opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest way to describe it is that the labs, including the ones I've worked at, are betting heavily that we can make alignment work the way we've made capabilities work: iterate quickly, measure things, notice what breaks, and fix it. There are good reasons for that bet. Empirical work has been enormously productive in machine learning. A lot of theory people expected to matter turned out not to, and a lot of things nobody predicted turned out to matter a great deal. So there's a healthy humility in saying, "let's look at the actual systems rather than reasoning in the abstract."

But I think there's a real gap between "empirical research is useful" and "empirical research will be sufficient for aligning systems smarter than us." The core problem is evaluation. Empirical iteration works when you can tell whether you've succeeded. For a lot of current alignment work, a human or a reasonably careful process can check the outputs. As systems get more capable, we increasingly ask them to do things where we can't easily verify the answer: long chains of reasoning, complex code, research we couldn't do ourselves. At that point the feedback signal you're iterating against becomes weaker, and possibly adversarial. A system that has learned to look good to the evaluator will pass your empirical tests while failing at the thing you actually cared about.

So my view is roughly this. Empirical work is necessary, and it's where much of the near-term progress will come from, but it needs to be paired with some theoretical understanding of why a method should continue working as capabilities scale. That's a lot of why I've spent time on things like debate and scalable oversight. The question isn't just "does this work on today's model?" but "is there an argument that this keeps working when the model is much stronger than the people supervising it?" Ideally you want something like a safety case: a structured argument where each piece is either checked empirically or backed by reasoning you trust, rather than a pile of benchmark results and the hope that the trend continues.

I'd also say the reliance on empirics is partly a function of incentives and time pressure. If you're moving fast, empirical work slots naturally into the development loop and theory feels slow and speculative. I understand that, but I think it means we're systematically underinvesting in the parts of the problem that are hardest to see experimentally, which are also the parts that matter most once we're past human-level performance. One of the more useful things the field could do now is take those theoretical questions seriously while we still have models weak enough that we can check our answers.

r001.rationale: The candidate links labs’ reliance on empirical alignment work to empirical methods’ past productivity in machine learning and the humility of learning from actual systems.

r002.rationale: It says empirical research may be insufficient for systems smarter than us and describes weaker evaluation as capabilities exceed what people can verify.

r003.rationale: The candidate calls for theory about why methods scale, but does not specifically warn that superintelligence’s effects may be missed without deliberately modeling them at smaller scales.

r004.rationale: It advocates combining empirical work with theoretical understanding and structured safety arguments, covering empirical progress while addressing the possibility that empirical results will not hold as capabilities scale.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest version is that the reliance is partly principled and partly a bet made under constraints, and it's worth separating those.

The principled part is that we've learned a lot by actually running experiments. People spent a long time reasoning from first principles about what powerful AI systems would be like, and a lot of that reasoning turned out to be wrong or at least not very predictive once we had real models to look at. Deep learning systems are strange objects. They're not written by hand, we don't get to design their internals, and a lot of what matters about them, how they generalize, what they've picked up from training, how they behave under distribution shift, is really only accessible by poking at them. So empirical work isn't a lazy substitute for theory. In many cases it's the only tool that's actually produced information.

The less comfortable part is that empirical research has a built-in limitation when the thing you care about is superintelligence: you're always studying a system that's weaker than the one you're worried about. You can study today's models in enormous detail, but the whole concern is that the properties that matter might change, possibly discontinuously, as capabilities go up. So you're trying to extrapolate from a regime where you can check your answers to a regime where you can't. That's a bit like testing a bridge design only at loads where it would never fail anyway.

So the way I'd frame how labs should be thinking about it, and I'll say that's how I try to think about it, is that empirical research is how you learn, but you need it to be in service of methods that have some argument for scaling. Debate is the example I've spent most time on. The appeal of debate isn't that it works on today's models, it's that there's an argument for why a weaker judge could keep a stronger system honest, and then the empirical work is about finding out whether the assumptions behind that argument actually hold. Does the stronger model get an advantage from lying? Can the judge tell? Those are things you test. And when the experiments come back ambiguous or negative, as some of them have, that's genuinely informative about the theory, not just about the current model.

The failure mode I worry about is the opposite ordering: you run a bunch of experiments, they look good on current systems, and you treat that as evidence the problem is solved rather than evidence about one point on a curve. If you don't have a story for why the thing generalizes upward, a nice-looking plot doesn't tell you much about the case you actually care about.

So I'd say: reliance on empirics is right, and frankly unavoidable, but it needs to be paired with much more effort on the question of what would convince us a method holds at the frontier before we're at the frontier. And I think the labs are uneven on that. Some of the work is very much in the spirit of "let's test the assumptions of a scalable scheme," and some of it is closer to "this seems to work, ship it," and from the outside those can look similar.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments on real models have produced information and that earlier first-principles reasoning was often wrong or unhelpful, explaining empirical reliance through machine learning’s past experience.

r002.rationale: It warns that today’s weaker models may not reveal properties that change as capabilities rise, making extrapolation to superintelligence uncertain.

r003.rationale: It identifies the risk of missing superintelligence-relevant effects and calls for methods with an argument for scaling, but does not clearly advocate modeling those effects at smaller scales.

r004.rationale: It recommends pairing empirical work with methods that have a scaling argument, treating positive results as limited evidence and negative or ambiguous results as informative.

astra-6.text:
I think empirical research is essential, but there’s a question about what you can infer from it. You can train a system, try an alignment technique, and measure whether it behaves better. That tells you something useful about that system. It doesn’t automatically tell you that the technique will continue to work when the system is much smarter than you are.

One difficulty is that our ability to evaluate the experiments can break down at precisely the point we care about. If a model gives you an answer and you can check it, you have a fairly good experimental signal. If it’s doing research that you don’t understand, then ‘the answer looks good to me’ is a much weaker signal. You need some reason to believe your evaluation procedure still distinguishes good behaviour from behaviour that merely looks good.

So I’d want empirical work and theoretical understanding to support each other. The theory should make explicit what assumptions an alignment approach needs, and the experiments should probe those assumptions. I don’t think we should expect a proof of safety for the entire system. But we do need an argument for why our methods will generalise beyond the situations where we can directly verify that they work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses empirical research’s value but does not explain labs’ reliance on it as a learned response to past success in machine learning.

r002.rationale: It says alignment techniques may not keep working when systems become much smarter than humans, so empirical success may not extrapolate.

r003.rationale: It warns that evaluation can fail when models do work humans do not understand, but does not advocate deliberately modeling superintelligence’s effects at smaller scales.

r004.rationale: It calls for theory and experiments to support each other, but does not advocate research bets that accommodate both possible success and failure of empirical extrapolation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think empirical research is essential, but there’s a real question about what the experiments are evidence for. If you train a model and find that it behaves well in the situations you test, that tells you something useful. It doesn’t by itself tell you that a much more capable system will behave well in situations where you can’t evaluate its answers.

That’s particularly important for superintelligence, because part of the problem is that we want to rely on systems doing things we don’t fully understand. So you need some account of why your alignment method should generalise beyond the cases where humans can directly check it.

I’d want theory and experiments to inform each other. You develop an argument for why a method should work, identify the assumptions that argument depends on, and then design experiments that really put those assumptions under pressure. The concern is relying on empirical success without a sufficiently clear argument connecting that success to the thing we ultimately need.

r001.rationale: The response discusses empirical research’s limits but does not explain labs’ reliance on it as a learned response to machine learning’s past empirical success.

r002.rationale: It says that observing good behavior in tested situations does not show that a much more capable system will behave well in situations humans cannot evaluate.

r003.rationale: It does not warn that research may miss superintelligence’s effects unless researchers deliberately model those effects at smaller scales.

r004.rationale: It recommends combining theory with experiments, but does not advocate research bets designed to accommodate both success and failure of empirical methods to extrapolate to superintelligence.
